query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) designed for high-temperature applications, a protective oxide layer forms and is retained because reactive elements such as Cr and/or Al preferentially diffuse via grain boundaries to the alloy surface. There they form a continuous, adherent, slow-growing oxide (e.g., Cr2O3 and/or Al2O3) that acts as a diffusion barrier for oxygen, thereby self-limiting further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a balanced mixture of reactive elements (e.g., Al and/or Cr) and non‐reactive elements, exhibiting a microstructure with a controllable grain boundary density (fine vs. coarse grains).
generation.intervention: Exposure to a high-temperature oxidizing environment (for example, isothermal oxidation in air in the range of 850–1050 °C) for an extended duration.
generation.conditions: Testing under controlled high-temperature conditions with samples that vary primarily in microstructural grain boundary density, while keeping bulk composition constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain boundaries that enhance the transport of reactive species (Al, Cr) from the bulk to the surface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the reactive elements in the alloy diffuse preferentially along grain boundaries to the surface. Their enrichment at the surface leads to the in situ formation of a uniform and adherent oxide layer (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3). Because these oxides grow slowly and act as a barrier to oxygen ingress, they protect the underlying alloy from rapid oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples with a higher density of grain boundaries (fine-grained microstructures) will exhibit a more uniform, continuous, and slower-growing protective oxide layer, evidenced by lower mass gain and less oxide spallation compared to coarse-grained samples. In contrast, alloys with less pronounced grain boundary networks may form less continuous oxide layers that allow accelerated oxidation.
generation.baseline: HEA samples with a similar bulk composition but with a coarser microstructure (lower grain boundary density) and/or a less favorable distribution of reactive elements.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected to be most relevant at high temperatures (850–1050 °C) in oxidizing environments and for alloy compositions that contain sufficient amounts of reactive elements (e.g., Al and/or Cr). HEAs lacking such elements may not follow the same mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative roles of grain boundary diffusion versus bulk diffusion in delivering reactive elements to the surface remain uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical bulk compositions but differing microstructures: one set with a fine-grained (high grain boundary density) structure and the other with a coarse-grained structure. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions and monitor the evolution of oxide layers.
measurements: Mass gain over time using thermogravimetric analysis
Oxide layer morphology and continuity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Phase identification of surface oxides via X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Elemental distribution at the surface using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained samples do not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate and a more continuous, adherent protective oxide layer compared to the coarse-grained samples, then the hypothesis that grain boundary–mediated diffusion of reactive elements governs protective oxide formation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
